title: Heat Wave
description: Use this list before summer and when the NWS issues heat alerts, to keep your household and at-risk neighbors safe from heat illness.

sources.title: Winter Storms Aren't Over: CPSC Warns of Deadly Carbon Monoxide Risks (generator placement)

items.text: Never leave a child, older adult, or pet in a parked car, even for a minute or with a window cracked
Learn heat stroke signs (confusion, slurred speech, fainting, seizures, very high temperature): call 911 and cool the person fast
Learn heat exhaustion signs (heavy sweating, cool clammy skin, dizziness, nausea, cramps): move to a cool place and cool down
Find your nearest cooling centers and air-conditioned public spaces and how to get there
Make a buddy plan to check on older relatives, neighbors living alone, and people with chronic illness at least twice a day
Service the air conditioner and clean or replace its filters before summer
Ask your doctor or pharmacist if any of your medicines raise heat risk or need cool storage
Stock water and drink often, even before you are thirsty; skip alcohol (ask your doctor if your fluids are limited)
Use fans with cool showers and damp cloths - fans alone cannot keep you safe in very high heat
Put up light-colored shades or reflective film on sun-facing windows; close blinds by day
Light, loose, light-colored clothing and a wide-brim hat
Schedule outdoor work and exercise for early morning or evening
Check the NWS HeatRisk forecast and heat alerts for your area daily during hot spells
Leave a phone, bag, or shoe in the back seat so you always check before locking the car; keep cars locked
Ice packs and cool wet towels ready for emergency cooling
Plan for a heat-driven power outage: move at-risk people somewhere cool early, and run generators only outdoors 20 feet (6 m) from openings
Keep pets inside with water and shade, and check that pavement is not too hot for their paws
Eat lighter meals and avoid using the oven during the hottest hours
